doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Chance connections: Soupy Sales and Pilar Arcos
summary: Jazz history is full of chance meetings; he describes researching Soupy Sales's jazz radio show and singer Pilar Arcos, Chuck Findley's wife's grandmother.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: just went on. The synchronicity thing also, you know there’s a lot of chance in the larger sense of the word, in the jazz world. Somebody gets — it’s like Lou Gehrig with the guy that couldn’t play first base that day, you know a person can’t make a gig, all right, they get a sub, and before you know it, if not subsequent to that but when the vocalist leaves that group and goes on to another one, boom he plucks up, you know, that player. So when you go back and you study and look at, if not study this stuff you see all of these sort of random meetings, events. It’s like the gal that got discovered at Schwab’s Pharmacy in Hollywood. I forget who it was, all right, but that kind of thing is absolutely fascinating and I mentioned before we were recording live, I’m doing a thing now on the comedian Soupy Sales. And a lot of people don’t know he was a great jazz lover and he had a radio show in Detroit in the 50s and the theme song was “Yardbird Suite” and Bird was on the show three times, and Miles was on six times, they’re all gone. Now Yusef Lateef, okay, and I happened to be talking to Pete Barbutti and I mentioned that I was doing this thing and Pete says, “Oh yeah,” he says, “I knew Soupy from before in Toledo. We’re old friends, we’ve been together.” The whole nine yards. So you have all of these sort of like circles. It’s sort of like a Venn diagram, you know, all of these things, all right? And then in some way, shape or form they come together. I’ll tell you another one that was really fascinating. Chuck Findley, who I’m sure you know, one of the great, great, great musicians and great people, I love him. He put something up on FaceBook about his wife’s grandmother apparently was a singer. So I thought this was kind of interesting and I would kind of scratch the surface. And the singer’s name was Pilar Arcos A-R-C-O-S. And Zelee, Chuck’s wife, that’s her grandmother. So anyway I start researching Pilar Arcos and as the dominoes fall one thing led to another, and you find out, if I recollect correctly, she came to the U.S. by way of Cuba although that’s not where she was originally from I don’t think. I don’t remember that part, came to the U.S. and was a vocalist and in the 20s, with the advent of I guess 78s, she was one of the foremost recorded artists in New York if not the U.S. And there were all of these recordings, primarily in Spanish, all right, that she sang and she was extremely famous, and she studied with a voice teacher and the person who would follow her or precede her in her lesson was Carlotta Monti who was W.C. Fields’ girlfriend. So and then of course it went on to Hollywood, Pilar went on to Hollywood with “I Love Lucy” and Ricardo Montalban and Cesar Romero and all these other people. But the crazy thing about these things is that it’s all this in some way, shape or form. Whether it’s the hand of God if you think that way as I do, or pure chance, you know this is how a lot of things have happened. And when you kind of dive in, you know which is really the fun thing. You know I must have been like a dachshund in a prior life trying to rat out the rats. But when you start researching this stuff and you turn a page and turn a page and it’s absolutely
amazing you know. And it has impact upon the artists and it has impact upon the artist’s music, which as a reviewer gives me more ammunition so to speak in terms of what the artist is all about.
I totally agree, that you’re being faithful to this person’s personality if you happen to know them, and I agree that this music isn’t made in a vacuum.
